original_value: Objective: The present experiment sought to examine the effects of event rate on a cognitive vigilance task. Background: Vigilance, or the ability to sustain attention, is an integral component of human factors research. Vigilance task difficulty has previously been manipulated through increasing event rate. However, most research in this paradigm has utilized a sensory-based task, whereas little work has focused on these effects in relation to a cognitive-based task. Method: In sum, 84 participants completed a cognitive vigilance task that contained either 24 events per minute (low event rate condition) or 40 events per minute (high event rate condition). Performance was measured through the proportion of hits, false alarms, mean response time, and signal detection analyses (i.e., sensitivity and response bias). Additionally, measures of perceived workload and stress were collected. Results: The results indicated that event rate significantly affected performance, such that participants who completed the low event rate task achieved significantly better performance in terms of correction detections and false alarms. Furthermore, the cognitive vigil utilized in the present study produced performance decrements comparable to traditional sensory vigilance tasks. Conclusion: Event rate affects cognitive vigilance tasks in a similar manner as traditional sensory vigilance tasks, such that a direct relation between performance and level of event rate was established. Application: Cognitive researchers wishing to manipulate task difficulty in their experiments may use event rate presentation as one avenue to achieve this result.

result.paraphrase: Objective: This experiment examined how event rate influences a cognitive vigilance task. Background: Vigilance, the capacity to maintain attention, is a key element of human factors research. Task difficulty in vigilance studies has often been manipulated by increasing event rate. However, most work in this area has used sensory tasks, with little research addressing these effects in cognitive tasks. Method: Eighty-four participants completed a cognitive vigilance task presented at either 24 events per minute (low event rate condition) or 40 events per minute (high event rate condition). Performance was assessed using hit proportion, false alarms, mean response time, and signal detection analyses, including sensitivity and response bias. Perceived workload and stress were also measured. Results: Event rate significantly influenced performance, with participants in the low event rate condition showing significantly better performance in correct detections and false alarms. In addition, the cognitive vigilance task used here produced performance declines comparable to those seen in traditional sensory vigilance tasks. Conclusion: Event rate affects cognitive vigilance tasks similarly to traditional sensory vigilance tasks, establishing a direct relationship between performance and event rate level. Application: Cognitive researchers looking to manipulate task difficulty in experiments may use event rate presentation as one way to do so.
